title: The Côte d'Or, Climat by Climat
subRegion: Côte de Nuits and Côte de Beaune, Burgundy

bestPeriod.note: Late September to mid-October overlaps harvest (vendange); domaines are busiest and some close tasting rooms for a week at a time.

summary: A week walking the Côte d'Or's Grand Cru and Premier Cru climats, from Beaune's covered market to domaines that answer email in weeks, not days.
hook: A single ridge, barely 60 km end to end, carries more named, legally defined vineyard parcels than anywhere else on earth — the climats, mapped by monks and refined for eight centuries, now a UNESCO World Heritage landscape. This week is built on foot and by train along that ridge, from the Côte de Nuits' reds down through Beaune to the Côte de Beaune's whites, with the market, the Hospices and the protocol for actually getting a domaine to say yes.

snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: Approx. 70 km by train and bike across the week; flat vineyard paths, 8–15 km per walking/cycling day
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to Lyon-Saint-Exupéry (LYS) or Paris; TGV to Le Creusot TGV or Dijon, then TER to Beaune (approx. 20 min)
snapshot.Who It Suits: Serious wine drinkers willing to email ahead and walk between villages rather than be driven

itinerary.title: Beaune, inside the ramparts
itinerary.morning: Arrive via TGV to Dijon or Le Creusot TGV, then the short TER connection into Beaune. Walk the old town's ramparts, the fortified circuit that still rings the centre, and get your bearings from the Place Carnot.
itinerary.afternoon: Approach the Hôtel-Dieu from outside first — the polychrome tile roof is the image everyone has of Beaune, and the courtyard is free to view. Save the interior museum for tomorrow.
itinerary.evening: Dinner near the ramparts: oeufs en meurette, poached eggs in a reduced red wine sauce with lardons and pearl onions, is the dish to start the week on. A village-level Beaune red or a Hautes-Côtes de Beaune sits well with it.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 0. Km travelled: 4. Approx. tasting spend: €15–€20.

itinerary.title: The market, and two walk-in cellars
itinerary.morning: Beaune's Saturday market fills Place Carnot and nearby streets from about 08:00 to 13:00 — cheese, produce, a proper crowd of locals. Structure the week so this day lands on a Saturday if you can; a smaller Wednesday market is the fallback.
itinerary.afternoon: Two walk-in tastings, no reservation needed: the Marché aux Vins, a cellar tasting cut into the town's old church crypts, and Patriarche Père et Fils, holder of the largest cellars in Burgundy — around 5 km of tunnels under the former Couvent des Visitandines — with a self-guided route through them.
itinerary.evening: Dinner: jambon persillé, a cold terrine of ham set in parsleyed white wine aspic, a Burgundian Easter dish served year-round in Beaune's better bistros.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 2 (walk-in). Km travelled: 5. Approx. tasting spend: €20–€30.

itinerary.title: Pommard and Volnay, on foot
itinerary.morning: Walk south from Beaune on the vineyard paths toward Pommard, about 4 km — the first village of the Côte de Beaune, known for structured, mineral reds. The path runs directly between the rows; note the small stone signs (bornes) marking where one climat ends and the next begins.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue to Volnay, another 3 km, through Premier Cru sites like Clos des Chênes and Caillerets. This is the practical way to learn the hierarchy: Bourgogne regional at the base, village appellation (Volnay, Pommard) above that, Premier Cru naming a specific parcel, and Grand Cru — the rarest tier, about 1% of production — reserved for a short list of the most prized sites.
itinerary.evening: Reservation tasting at a small Pommard or Volnay domaine, booked by email 4–6 weeks ahead, or via the Beaune tourist office's list of domaines open to visitors. Expect a modest fee and a real expectation you'll buy a bottle or two.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 1. Km travelled: 14 (round trip). Approx. tasting spend: €25–€40.

itinerary.title: Clos de Vougeot and the Côte de Nuits
itinerary.morning: TER train north from Beaune to Vougeot (about 12 minutes), then walk to the Château du Clos de Vougeot — seat of the Confrérie des Chevaliers du Tastevin and the walled Grand Cru vineyard itself, one of the Côte de Nuits' oldest sites, planted by Cistercian monks. The château interior is open without reservation, small entrance fee.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue on foot or by local bus to Vosne-Romanée. You will not get inside Domaine de la Romanée-Conti — it receives no public visitors, and that scarcity is itself the lesson: some of Burgundy's most quoted names are not for sale as an experience, only as a very expensive bottle. Walk the lane past the Romanée-Conti and La Tâche parcels from the public road instead.
itinerary.evening: Reservation tasting at Domaine Faiveley in Nuits-Saint-Georges, booked several weeks ahead by email — a long-established, serious Côte de Nuits house that does receive visitors in a proper cellar setting.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 1 (plus Clos de Vougeot château). Km travelled: 10. Approx. tasting spend: €30–€45.

itinerary.title: Gevrey-Chambertin, and Dijon's mustard
itinerary.morning: Train to Gevrey-Chambertin, home to nine Grand Cru climats including Chambertin itself, the vineyard Napoleon reportedly never travelled without. Walk the short loop through the village and up into the lower rows.
itinerary.afternoon: Continue by train to Dijon, 20 minutes further north, for a change of register: the Maille boutique on Rue de la Liberté sells mustard drawn straight from the tap, an old Dijon tradition, and the half-timbered old town is worth an unhurried two hours.
itinerary.evening: Back to Beaune. Dinner built around Époisses, the pungent washed-rind cheese from a village 30 minutes northwest, paired with a structured Gevrey-Chambertin.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 0 (village walking + Dijon). Km travelled: 45 (rail). Approx. tasting spend: €10–€15.

itinerary.title: Cycling the Côte de Beaune
itinerary.morning: Rent a bike in Beaune and ride the Voie des Vignes, the region's dedicated vineyard cycle route, south toward Santenay — about 16 km one-way, quiet lanes and greenway, flat and well-signed.
itinerary.afternoon: Stop in Chassagne-Montrachet and Puligny-Montrachet, straddling the Grand Cru Montrachet vineyard — split between the two communes, considered by many the finest dry white vineyard anywhere. A reservation tasting at a village-level producer (arranged by email in advance) is more realistic than any Grand Cru bottle, but standing at the parcel's edge is worth the ride alone.
itinerary.evening: Return to Beaune by bike or by folding the bike onto a TER service. Dinner: coq au vin, the other Burgundian standard, paired with a Chassagne-Montrachet white if the day's tasting has put you in the mood for more.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 1. Km travelled: 32 (round trip cycling). Approx. tasting spend: €25–€35.

itinerary.title: Last cellar, and out
itinerary.morning: A final reservation tasting somewhere you didn't reach earlier in the week — Bouchard Père & Fils or Louis Jadot in Beaune both run structured cellar visits by appointment, and take bookings a day or two ahead outside peak season.
itinerary.afternoon: Buy at the source: most domaines ship, but a hand-carried case is part of the week for most visitors.
itinerary.evening: TER to Dijon or Le Creusot TGV, connecting onward to Lyon or Paris for the flight home.
itinerary.dayStats: Cellars visited: 1. Km travelled: 40 (rail). Approx. tasting spend: €30–€50.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hôtel Le Cep
accommodationStrategy.description: A cluster of 16th- and 17th-century buildings inside the ramparts, a short walk from the Hôtel-Dieu, the market square and the station — the best-located base for a week run almost entirely on foot and rail.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hôtel des Remparts
accommodationStrategy.description: A quieter courtyard hotel a few streets from Place Carnot, useful if Le Cep's rates push the budget too far while keeping the same walkable position.

accommodationStrategy.name: A chambre d'hôtes in Pommard or Volnay
accommodationStrategy.description: Trades city convenience for waking inside the vineyard rows; a fair alternative for the middle nights if you'd rather walk to a domaine than take a train. Confirm the owner can store bikes and bottles securely.

logistics.emergency: 112 pan-European; also 15 (SAMU medical), 17 (police), 18 (fire) work directly in France.
logistics.weather: Summer afternoons on the open vineyard paths offer no shade at all; carry water on the Pommard–Volnay and Voie des Vignes days.
logistics.bookingWindows: Email 4–6 weeks ahead in French or English; state party size and whether you plan to buy. The Beaune Office de Tourisme and the BIVB (Bureau Interprofessionnel des Vins de Bourgogne) both maintain lists of domaines currently open to visitors and can relay requests to smaller producers.
logistics.money: Cards are accepted everywhere in Beaune; smaller cellar-door sales sometimes prefer cash for round numbers.

other.label: Minimum spend
other.text: Small domaines rarely charge a hard tasting fee but expect a purchase; treat €40–€80 in bottles as the unwritten cost of a good visit.

other.label: Drink-drive alternative
other.text: Do not rent a car. The TER Dijon–Beaune–Chalon-sur-Saône line stops at or near most villages named here (Vougeot, Nuits-Saint-Georges, Gevrey-Chambertin), and the Voie des Vignes cycle route covers the Côte de Beaune villages Beaune does not reach by rail.

other.label: Opening-hour traps
other.text: Harvest (usually mid-September to early October) can close small domaines' tasting rooms without much notice — confirm the week of your visit, not just when you first book.

proTips: Learn the hierarchy before Day 3: regional, village, Premier Cru, Grand Cru. Every list and domaine explains itself in these terms — the fastest way to read a Burgundy label correctly.
Walk past Romanée-Conti's vines deliberately — how small and unremarkable the parcel looks against its reputation is itself the point of Day 4.
Visit the Hôtel-Dieu interior late morning; tour groups cluster earlier and the museum is far quieter after 11:30.
At Patriarche, walk the route slowly — the tasting cup (tastevin) given at the start is yours to keep, and refills are unlimited within it.
Rent bikes the evening before the Voie des Vignes day; ramparts shops run low on good bikes by 09:30 in peak season.
Ask any domaine whether they're a récoltant (grower-producer) or buy in grapes — it changes what you're tasting, and most are glad to explain it.

packingNotes: Comfortable walking shoes for vineyard paths that turn to packed dirt or light gravel.
A sunhat; the Côte's open rows offer almost no shade between villages.
A soft-sided wine bag or two, or ship bottles home via a domaine's export service rather than carrying a full case.
Smart-casual layers for evening — Beaune's better restaurants expect more than trail wear.
A phrasebook or app; smaller domaines outside Beaune are less consistently English-speaking than the town itself.
A printed copy of tasting confirmations; rural cellar signal can be unreliable.
whatCouldGoWrong: **A reservation-only domaine doesn't reply.** Fall back to Beaune's walk-in cellars (Patriarche, Marché aux Vins, Bouchard) — genuinely serious tastings without an appointment.
**Harvest closes a domaine mid-visit-window.** This is normal in late September; the Beaune tourist office can usually redirect you same-day to an open alternative.

**Rain washes out the Pommard–Volnay walk or the Voie des Vignes ride.** Both routes are entirely rideable/walkable in light rain with a shell jacket; heavier rain, retreat to Beaune's covered cellars for the day.
**You've bought more wine than you can carry.** Most domaines and the Beaune tourist office can point you to a shipping service; do not attempt to drive it out yourself if you didn't rent a car.
